source_text:
In Genesim (sermo 1) (olim sub auctore Joanne Chrysostomo)
Λόγος εἰς τὸ, "Εἶδεν ὁ Θεὸς πάντα ὅσα ἐποίησε· καὶ ἰδοὺ καλὰ λίαν·" καὶ
ὅτι τὰ θεῖα λόγια τιμιώτερα πάντων ἡδέων.
αʹ. Καλοὶ τῆς εὐσεβείας οἱ λειμῶνες, οὐ προσκαίροις χροιαῖς κομῶντες, ἀλλ'
οὐρανίοις ἄνθεσι βρύοντες. Ἄνθη δέ εἰσι τῆς εὐσεβείας, οἱ καρποὶ τῆς ἐνθέου
πολιτείας. Αἱ γὰρ ἀρεταὶ ἀνάγουσιν ἡμᾶς εἰς τὸ θαυμαστὸν καὶ πρωτότυπον ἐκεῖνο
κάλλος τὸ κατ' εἰκόνα Θεοῦ γεγενημένον καὶ καθ' ὁμοίωσιν. Αὕτη τοίνυν ἡ κατ'
ἀρετὴν ὁμοίωσις ἵππον ἀντὶ ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἐᾷ λέγεσθαι. Ταύτην οὖν ὅταν
μεταδιώκωμεν, οὐκ ἔτι λύκος καὶ δράκων καὶ ὄφις καὶ σκορπίος ὀνομαζόμεθα, πρὸς
τὴν τῶν ἀλόγων ὕβριν καταφερόμενοι· ἀλλ' εἰκὼν Θεοῦ θαυμαστὴ καὶ τιμία, τὸ
πρωτότυπον κάλλος τοῦ χαρακτῆρος σώζουσα, καὶ ἐσμὲν, καὶ λεγόμεθα, καὶ
πιστευόμεθα. ∆εσπότης ἐγένου τῶν ἀλόγων· μὴ μιμοῦ τῶν οἰκετῶν τὰ ἤθη· οὐκ
ἐπειδὴ φαῦλα τὰ ἄλογα· οὐδὲν γὰρ παρὰ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ κακὸν ἐκτίσθη. Μὴ γάρ τις
νομιζέτω ἐν χώρᾳ κακίας τὰ ἄλογα τάττεσθαι, διὰ τὸ εἰκόνα κακίας παρῆχθαι τῶν
μὴ κατ' ἀρετὴν βιούντων. Εἰ γὰρ τοῦτο, πῶς εἶπεν ἡ Γραφὴ, Καὶ εἶδεν ὁ Θεὸς πάντα
ὅσα ἐποίησε, καὶ ἰδοὺ καλὰ, καὶ οὐχ ἁπλῶς καλὰ, ἀλλὰ καὶ καλὰ λίαν; Ὁπότε οὖν τὰ
γεγονότα εἰς εἰκόνα κακίας παρήχθησαν (ὁ γὰρ λέων εἰκὼν τοῦ τυράννου, καὶ ὁ
ὄφις τοῦ σκολιοῦ καὶ τοῦ πονηροτάτου τὸν τρόπον, καὶ ὁ σκορπίος τοῦ πλήκτου, καὶ
ὁ λύκος τοῦ ἁρπακτικοῦ), ποῦ ἂν εἴη καλὰ τὰ γενόμενα, φησὶν, οὕτω προφανῶς εἰς
εἰκόνα κακίας παραλαμβανόμενα; ∆εῖ δὲ εἰδέναι τοὺς φιλομαθεῖς, ὅτι ταῦτα τῇ
οἰκείᾳ φύσει κακὰ οὔτ' ἔστιν, οὔτε λέγεται, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ἀλόγοις πρέπουσα κατάστασις·
ἐπειδὰν δὲ ἔλθῃ εἰς τὴν λογικὴν φύσιν, ὑβρίζει τὴν θέαν, καὶ ἀμβλύνει τὴν λογικὴν
ἐλευθερίαν. Ἔλαβες, ἄνθρωπε, τὴν δεσποτικὴν ἀξίαν· μὴ τὴν ἄτιμον καὶ
δουλοπρεπῆ τῶν ἀλόγων μεταδίωκε τάξιν· ὑβρίζεις γὰρ σαυτὸν, μιμούμενος τῶν
ἀλόγων τὴν θηριωδίαν· οὐχ ὡς τῶν ἀλόγων κακῶν ὄντων, ἢ λεγομένων, ἀλλ' ὡς
τῆς ἀτίμου καὶ δουλοπρεποῦς εἰκόνος οὐ πρεπούσης τοῖς ἐλευθέροις. Ὥσπερ γάρ τις
ἀνὴρ ἐπίσημος καὶ ἐπίδοξος, ἐὰν ἐνδύσηται ἢ περιβάληται δούλου στολὴν, ὑβρίζεται,
καὶ καταισχύνεται, οὐχ ὡς τῆς ἐσθῆτος οὔσης φαύλης καὶ ῥυπαρᾶς, ἀλλ' ὡς δούλῳ
μὲν πρεπούσης, ἐλευθέρῳ δὲ μὴ ἁρμοττούσης· οὕτως ἐὰν ἦθος σκορπίου καὶ λύκου
ἀναλάβῃς, οὐχ ἡ φύσις τῶν ἀλόγων διαβάλλεται, ἀλλ' ἡ σὴ κατάστασις ὑβρίζεται ἡ
δεσποτείαν λαχοῦσα, καὶ τὰ δούλου μεταδιώκουσα. Ταῦτα δέ μοι ἀναγκαίως
παρῆκται, ἵνα μηδεὶς εἰς ὕβριν τῆς δημιουργίας ἐκλάβῃ τὰ εἰρημένα, ὡς τοῦ Θεοῦ
φαῦλόν τι πεποιηκότος· πάντα γὰρ ἀληθῶς καλὰ, καὶ καλὰ λίαν, ἐὰν τὴν οἰκείαν
φυλάττῃ τάξιν, καὶ τὸν οἰκεῖον μεταδιώκῃ νόμον. Ἵνα δὲ μάθῃς, ἀγαπητὲ, ὅτι οὐδὲν
φαῦλον γεγένηται παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ κατὰ φύσιν, ἐδίδαξεν ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεὸς καὶ τῶν ἀλόγων
τούτων εἰκόνα λαμβάνειν. Ὑπέθηκε γάρ τινα μιμεῖσθαι τῶν ἀλόγων
πλεονεκτήματα, ἵνα μὴ διαβάλλωμεν εἰς κακίαν τὰ γεγονότα, οὐ καθόλου τὴν
φύσιν, ἀλλ' ὅσα ἁρμόζει λογικῇ καταστάσει. Ἢ οὐκ ἤκουσας σήμερον τοῦ
Παροιμιαστοῦ λέγοντος, Πορεύθητι πρὸς τὸν μύρμηκα, ὀκνηρὲ, καὶ ζήλωσον τὰς
ὁδοὺς αὐτοῦ; Οὐ συνῆκας πῶς τὴν τοῦ μύρμηκος φιλοπονίαν ὑποθέμενος, εἰς
ἄοκνον ἡμῶν προθυμίαν ἐπαιδαγώγησεν;
thought_title: The meadow of piety and the good creation of irrational animals
orientation: The homily opens by praising the virtues as the meadow of piety that restores the image of God, then defends the goodness of irrational animals against those who would call them evil because Scripture uses them as images of vice.
pass_a_gloss: Beautiful are the meadows of piety, not luxuriating with temporary colors, but blooming with heavenly flowers. And flowers of piety are the fruits of the inspired way of life. For the virtues lead us up to that wonderful and archetypal beauty, the one made according to the image of God and according to likeness. This likeness according to virtue, then, does not allow a horse to be said instead of a human. Therefore, whenever we pursue this, we are no longer called wolf and dragon and serpent and scorpion, being carried down to the insult of the irrational animals; but a wonderful and honored image of God, preserving the archetypal beauty of the character, we both are, and are called, and are believed to be. You became master of the irrational animals; do not imitate the ways of the servants; not because the irrational animals are base; for nothing evil was created by the good one. For let no one suppose that the irrational animals are placed in the region of wickedness, because an image of wickedness has been produced from those who do not live according to virtue. For if this is so, how did Scripture say, And God saw all things that he made, and behold, good, and not simply good, but also very good? Since therefore the things that came to be were produced as an image of wickedness (for the lion is an image of the tyrant, and the serpent of the crooked and most wicked one in manner, and the scorpion of the striker, and the wolf of the rapacious one), where would the things that came to be be good, he says, being so manifestly taken as an image of wickedness? But the lovers of learning must know that these things by their own nature are neither evil nor are called evil, but a condition befitting the irrational animals; but whenever it comes into the rational nature, it insults the sight, and dulls the rational freedom. You received, O human, the masterly dignity; do not pursue the dishonored and slavish rank of the irrational animals; for you insult yourself, imitating the savagery of the irrational animals; not as though the irrational animals are evil, or are called evil, but as though the dishonored and slavish image is not fitting for the free. For just as a certain distinguished and renowned man, if he puts on or wraps himself in a slave's garment, is insulted and put to shame, not as though the clothing is base and filthy, but as though it befits a slave, but does not suit a free man; so if you take up the manner of a scorpion and a wolf, not the nature of the irrational animals is slandered, but your condition is insulted, the one that obtained mastery, and pursues the things of a slave. And these things have been brought forward by me necessarily, so that no one may take the things said as an insult to the creation, as though God had made something base; for all things are truly good, and very good, if each keeps its own order, and pursues its own law. And so that you may learn, beloved, that nothing base has come to be from God according to nature, God taught us to take an image even from these irrational animals. For he set before us certain excellent qualities of the irrational animals to imitate, so that we may not slander the things that came to be into wickedness, not the nature as a whole, but as many things as befit a rational condition. Or did you not hear today the Proverbist saying, Go to the ant, O sluggard, and emulate his ways? Did you not understand how, setting before us the diligence of the ant, he led us by instruction to unhesitating eagerness?

choices.why: Fixed glossary term for reverent devotion to God, the meadow in which virtues bloom.
Fixed glossary term; the path of likeness to God, not generic excellence.
Fixed glossary term for the image of God in humanity restored by virtue.
Fixed glossary term for likeness to God achieved through virtue.
Fixed glossary term; created good but used as images of vice.
Fixed glossary term for a useful or excellent quality of an animal that can be imitated.

pass_b_english: The meadows of piety are beautiful—not because they are adorned with colors that fade, but because they bloom with heavenly flowers. And the flowers of piety are the fruits of a life inspired by God. For the virtues lead us up to that wonderful, original beauty that was made according to the image of God and according to his likeness. This likeness through virtue, then, does not allow us to be called a horse instead of a human being. So when we pursue it, we are no longer named wolf and dragon and snake and scorpion, dragged down into the insult of the irrational animals. Instead, we are—and are called, and are believed to be—a wonderful and precious image of God, preserving the original beauty of the stamp. You became master of the irrational animals; do not imitate the ways of your servants. Not because the irrational animals are worthless—nothing evil was created by the Good One. Let no one suppose that the irrational animals are placed in the territory of evil, just because they have been brought forward as an image of evil for those who do not live according to virtue. If that were so, how could Scripture say, “God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was good”—and not simply good, but “very good” (Genesis 1:31)? Since the things that were made have been brought forward as images of evil—the lion as an image of the tyrant, the snake of the crooked and most wicked in character, the scorpion of the one who strikes, the wolf of the grasping man—where, someone says, would the things that were made be good, when they are so openly taken up as images of evil? But those who love learning must understand this: these things are not evil by their own nature, nor are they called evil. They are a condition that suits the irrational animals. But when that condition comes into a rational nature, it insults the sight and dulls rational freedom. You received, O human being, the dignity of a master. Do not pursue the dishonorable, slavish rank of the irrational animals. For you insult yourself when you imitate the savagery of the irrational animals—not because the irrational animals are evil or are called evil, but because a dishonorable and slavish image does not suit those who are free. Just as a distinguished and renowned man, if he puts on or wraps himself in a slave's garment, is insulted and disgraced—not because the clothing is worthless and filthy, but because it suits a slave and does not fit a free man—so too, if you take on the character of a scorpion and a wolf, the nature of the irrational animals is not slandered; rather, your own condition is insulted—the condition that received mastery and yet pursues the things of a slave. I have brought these points forward out of necessity, so that no one may take what has been said as an insult to creation, as though God had made something worthless. For all things are truly good, and very good, if each keeps its own order and pursues its own law. And so that you may learn, beloved, that nothing worthless by nature has been made by God, God has taught us to take an image even from these irrational animals. For he has set before us certain excellent qualities of the irrational animals to imitate, so that we may not slander what has been made as evil—not the whole nature, but only what suits a rational condition. Did you not hear today the author of Proverbs saying, “Go to the ant, you sluggard, and imitate his ways” (Proverbs 6:6)? Did you not understand how, by setting before us the diligence of the ant, he trained us toward unhesitating eagerness?

last_rejected.quote: And the flowers of piety are the fruits of a life inspired by God.
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἄνθη δέ εἰσι τῆς εὐσεβείας, οἱ καρποὶ τῆς ἐνθέου πολιτείας.
last_rejected.why: Greek says the fruits of the inner civic life, not a life inspired by God.
last_rejected.fix: And the flowers of piety are the fruits of the inner civic life.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐνθέου means 'divinely inspired' or 'inspired by God'; 'inner civic life' is wrong. Translation is correct.

last_rejected.quote: when that condition comes into a rational nature, it insults the sight and dulls rational freedom.
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐπειδὰν δὲ ἔλθῃ εἰς τὴν λογικὴν φύσιν, ὑβρίζει τὴν θέαν, καὶ ἀμβλύνει τὴν λογικὴν ἐλευθερίαν.
last_rejected.why: Greek says it offends death (θέαν), not “the sight”.
last_rejected.fix: when that condition comes into a rational nature, it offends death and dulls rational freedom.
last_rejected.ruling: θέαν is accusative singular of θέα ('sight', 'spectacle'), not θάνατος ('death'). 'The sight' is correct.

last_rejected.quote: Not because the irrational animals are worthless—nothing evil was created by the Good One.
last_rejected.source_quote: Μὴ γάρ τις νομιζέτω ἐν χώρᾳ κακίας τὰ ἄλογα τάττεσθαι, διὰ τὸ εἰκόνα κακίας παρῆχθαι τῶν μὴ κατ' ἀρετὴν βιούντων.
last_rejected.why: The source denies placing irrational animals in the realm of evil, not that they are “worthless”.
last_rejected.fix: Not because the irrational animals are placed in the realm of evil—nothing evil was created by the Good One.
last_rejected.ruling: φαῦλα at line 12 means 'worthless'/'bad'; the English rendering captures the argument accurately.
